title: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR)
summary: Specifies CBOR, the Concise Binary Object Representation, a data format designed for very small code size, fairly small messages, and extensibility without version negotiation. This revision obsoletes RFC 7049, providing editorial fixes, clarifications, and some small additions while keeping the format compatible. It is an Internet Standard.

eli5.summary: CBOR is like JSON's compact cousin: a way for computers to pack up data into very small messages that are still easy to unpack.

questions: what are the cbor major types
what is the cbor media type
subtitle: A compact, self-describing binary data format built from the JSON data model, for tiny code and small messages.

tldr.problem: Constrained devices and high-volume systems need to exchange structured data, but text formats like JSON are bulky and existing binary formats such as ASN.1 do not fit goals of tiny code, no schema and room to grow.
tldr.mechanism: CBOR starts from an extended JSON data model and encodes every item with an initial byte holding a 3-bit major type and 5 bits of additional information, followed by any length or value bytes. Tags and simple values provide extensibility.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8949 is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 7049 with editorial fixes and clarifications, keeping full compatibility with the earlier format. It does not create a new version of the format.

today: RFC 8949 is an Internet Standard (STD 94). It obsoletes RFC 7049 and keeps full compatibility with that format, so it is the current definition of CBOR.

sections.title: Goals of CBOR
sections.content:
Hundreds of binary serialization formats exist. CBOR, the Concise Binary Object Representation, was designed for goals the existing ones meet poorly. Its data model is an extended version of the JSON data model, but the RFC is explicit that this is not a proposal to extend JSON itself.

The objectives, roughly in decreasing order of importance, are: unambiguously encode the common data formats of Internet standards; keep encoder and decoder code small enough for very constrained devices; decode without a schema (data is self-describing); be reasonably compact, though code size matters more than message size; suit both constrained nodes and high-volume applications; support all JSON data types for conversion; and be extensible so that extended data is still decodable by earlier decoders, in a format designed for decades of use.

Notably, there is no requirement that data be uniquely encoded: the number 7 may be encoded in several ways. All multi-byte values use network byte order (big-endian).
sections.eli5: Imagine a way to write notes using very few letters so even a tiny toy robot can read them, yet any robot can understand a note without asking what the code means.

sections.title: The CBOR Data Model
sections.content:
CBOR separates a generic data model from its byte encoding. In the basic model a data item is one of: an integer in the range -2^64 to 2^64-1; a simple value identified by a number from 0 to 255; a floating-point value (IEEE 754 binary64, including non-finites); a byte string; a text string of Unicode code points; an array; a map of key and value pairs; or a tagged item made of a tag number and tag content. Integers and floats are distinct even when numerically equal.

The model is extended by registering simple values and tag numbers. It never shrinks. Examples include false, true, null and undefined (simple values 20 to 23) and date/time and big number tags. An application then picks a subset as its own specific data model, which may declare, for example, that 1 and 1.0 are equivalent map keys.

The RFC layers acceptability: an item is well-formed if it follows the syntax, valid if it also obeys CBOR's semantic rules, and expected if it meets the application's own requirements.
sections.eli5: CBOR has a set of building blocks: numbers, words, lists, labeled boxes, and a few special yes/no/nothing tokens. You can combine them into whatever message you need.

sections.title: How Items Are Encoded
sections.content:
Every encoded item starts with an initial byte. Its high-order 3 bits are the major type and its low-order 5 bits are additional information. Usually the additional information gives an argument: below 24 it is the value itself; 24, 25, 26 or 27 mean the value follows in 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes; 28 to 30 are reserved and make an item not well-formed; 31 means indefinite length. For example, the integer 500 is 0b000_11001 followed by the two bytes 0x01f4.

The eight major types are unsigned integer (0), negative integer (1, value is -1 minus the argument), byte string (2), UTF-8 text string (3), array (4), map (5), tag (6) and floating-point or simple value (7). Text is never escaped, so a newline is always the byte 0x0a.

Arrays, maps, byte strings and text strings may use indefinite length so an encoder can start before it knows the size. Such an item ends with the break stop code 0xff. Indefinite-length strings are made of definite-length chunks and cannot nest.

Major type 7 carries floats: additional information 25, 26 and 27 are 16-bit, 32-bit and 64-bit IEEE 754 values. Simple values 20, 21, 22 and 23 are false, true, null and undefined.
sections.eli5: The first byte is a label on the front of each little package saying what kind it is and how big. After that comes the package contents, so a reader never needs a separate instruction sheet.

sections.title: Tags and Future Growth
sections.content:
A tag wraps a data item and gives it extra meaning through a tag number. Decoders need not understand every tag; they can hand the tag number and content to the application. The main purpose of the tags in this document is to define common data types such as dates.

  • Tag 0: date/time text string in RFC 3339 form. Tag 1: seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00Z, as an integer or float.
  • Tags 2 and 3: unsigned and negative big numbers, carried as byte strings. Tags 4 and 5: decimal fractions and bigfloats, carried as an array of an exponent and a mantissa.
  • Tags 21 to 23: hints for later conversion to base64url, base64 and base16. Tag 24: an embedded, encoded CBOR data item.
  • Tags 32, 33, 34 and 36: URI, base64url text, base64 text and MIME message.
  • Tag 55799: self-described CBOR, whose head serializes as 0xd9d9f7, useful at the start of stored data.

CBOR has three major extension points: the simple value space, the tag space, and the additional information space. The last is hard to extend because a decoder meeting an unknown value cannot keep decoding, and very few values are left. Values 28 and 29 are viewed as candidates for 128-bit and 256-bit quantities, and only value 30 remains for general allocation.
sections.eli5: A tag is a sticky note on a package that says "this is a date" or "this is a really big number." If you do not know the sticky note, you can still open the package.

sections.title: Preferred and Deterministic Encoding
sections.content:
Because CBOR often has several valid encodings for one value, the RFC defines preferred serialization: use the shortest form for each argument, the shortest floating-point encoding that preserves the value (for example 0xf94580 for 5.5), and definite length when the length is known up front. Neither encoders nor decoders are forced to follow it, but a preferred encoder interoperates better with constrained decoders.

Protocols that need a single canonical byte string can use core deterministic encoding. It requires preferred serialization, forbids indefinite-length items, and sorts the keys of every map in bytewise lexicographic order of their deterministic encodings. A "length-first" variant sorts shorter keys first, for compatibility with the ordering suggested in RFC 7049. The RFC avoids the term "Canonical CBOR" but says the terms are essentially interchangeable.

Section 5 adds advice for protocol designers: a CBOR-based protocol MUST say how decoders treat invalid and unexpected data, and MUST define what to do about duplicate map keys. Maps carry no meaning in key order. Using small integers as keys is suggested for constrained devices, since 24 or fewer keys fit in one byte each.
sections.eli5: There are many ways to write the same number, like "7" or "007". The preferred way is the shortest one. For deterministic encoding, everyone agrees on one exact way so two people always get identical results.

sections.title: Converting To and From JSON
sections.content:
The RFC gives non-normative advice for converters, which may use whichever of it they want. Going from CBOR to JSON, integers, text strings, arrays, maps, booleans and null map directly. Byte strings become base64url text without padding, big numbers become base64url strings (with a "~" prefix for negative ones), and non-finite floats or unassigned simple values become a substitute value such as null. Maps convert directly only when all keys are text strings, and converting other keys risks collisions.

Going from JSON to CBOR, integers use the shortest form, by default in the range -2^53+1 to 2^53-1, and numbers with fractions become floating-point values using the shortest exact form. The RFC warns that converting in place in a single buffer has pathological cases where output can grow, and mistakes there may be exploited by an attacker.

For humans, section 8 defines a diagnostic notation loosely based on JSON, such as 0("2013-03-21T20:04:00Z") for a tagged date and h'12345678' for a byte string. It is for documentation and debugging, not for interchange.
sections.eli5: CBOR and JSON can translate for each other, but some CBOR things have no JSON word, so the translator has to use a stand-in or spell them out in a special way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Decoders are often the first step in handling unvalidated input, so the RFC says a decoder must assume all input may be hostile, even if it came over a secure channel such as TLS or was signed. Hostile data can try to overrun buffers, overflow integer arithmetic, claim enormous sizes, or nest items deeply to exhaust the stack. Superlinear effort is also a risk, such as attackable hash tables used for maps and arbitrary-precision numbers.

Well-formedness is the first line of defense: input that is not well-formed gets no further processing. Validity checks may be done by the decoder or left to the application, but the choice must be documented. A key danger is multiple interpretations: duplicate map keys, a constrained decoder meeting a non-preferred serialization, or an integer sent as a bignum can be read differently by two components. Protocols should reduce these to a single interpretation, and applications should specify which data model they use. Converting CBOR to less expressive formats can also lose type information.
sections.eli5: A mail sorter should treat every envelope as possibly tricky, even from a trusted street. Check that it is shaped right, not impossibly huge, and that it means the same thing to everyone who reads it.

sections.title: Registries and Media Types
sections.content:
IANA created two separate registries: CBOR Simple Values and CBOR Tags. New simple values 0 to 19 need Standards Action, and 32 to 255 need Specification Required. For tags, 0 to 23 need Standards Action, 24 to 255 and 256 to 32767 need Specification Required, and 32768 to 18446744073709551615 are First Come First Served.

The media type for a single encoded CBOR item is application/cbor, with file extension .cbor. The CoAP Content-Format ID for it is 60, and the structured syntax suffix for media types built on CBOR is +cbor.
sections.eli5: There is a public list where new special tokens and sticky-note types get signed up, so nobody picks the same one twice. CBOR also got its own official file label.

items.label: Map
items.desc: N key and value pairs, 2N items, follow.

items.desc: Tag number N, then one data item.

items.desc: Simple values, floats and the break stop code.
